about: Design and Professional Skills I (Mechanical Engineering) is the mechanical engineering version of the Integrated Engineering Programme's Year 1 design-and-skills module, running across Terms 1 and 2. UCL describes a common syllabus delivered through each discipline: communication, ethics, teamwork and leadership, the engineering design cycle, and technical skills such as engineering drawing, CAD, programming and risk assessment, starting with the first-week Pebble in the Pond project and including week-long Scenarios. This guide does not state credits or an assessment breakdown; check the UCL Module Catalogue and Moodle for your year. This guide explains the module and the standard drawing, ethics and risk content it draws on; it does not invent a syllabus.

notes.h: What Design and Professional Skills I is
notes.body:
Design and Professional Skills I (DPS I) is the design-and-skills strand of UCL's Integrated Engineering Programme (IEP) in Year 1. Every IEP department runs its own version; ENGF0033 is the Mechanical Engineering version. According to UCL Engineering's "How we teach" page, DPS runs across Terms 1 and 2 of the first year and continues as DPS II in the second year.

What it covers
UCL's IEP pages describe a common syllabus that each department delivers through its own discipline, with mechanical engineering examples in your case. The areas named are:
- communication;
- ethics, professional standards and sustainability;
- legal and management concepts;
- risk and safety, including risk assessment;
- creative and critical thinking, and decision making;
- teamwork and leadership;
- the engineering design cycle;
- technical skills such as engineering drawing, CAD and programming.

Design is the thread that ties these together: the skills are taught so that you can apply them in design projects.

How it fits with other Year 1 modules
- It opens with a first-week project called Pebble in the Pond (see the next note).
- It includes Scenarios: week-long team design projects in which other lectures stop so that you can focus on one technical problem.
- In Term 1 it runs alongside Engineering Challenges (ENGF0001) and Mathematical Modelling and Analysis I, and the IEP cross-references material between these modules.

Assessment
This guide does not state an assessment breakdown or credit value for ENGF0033. Check the module's entry in the UCL Module Catalogue and your Moodle page for the current pattern, deadlines and marking criteria. Because DPS is taught through workshops and projects, deliverables such as reports, drawings and presentations are likely, but this guide could not confirm the assessment pattern, so check it for your year.

How to prepare
- Get used to sketching: quick freehand isometric and orthographic sketches of everyday objects (a stapler, a bottle opener) build the visual skills that drawing and CAD rely on.
- Learn the basics of one CAD package if you can get access, so that the first sessions are about technique rather than finding buttons.
- Read the current Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering Statement of Ethical Principles (updated February 2026) so that ethics discussions start from the profession's own framework.
- Start a design logbook from day one: dated sketches, calculations, decisions and sources. It is the raw material for reports and reflections.

Exam tips: in any DPS deliverable, show the reasoning behind decisions (requirements, alternatives considered, criteria and evidence) rather than just the final design.

notes.h: Pebble in the Pond and the Scenarios
notes.body:
Two features of DPS I are distinctive to UCL's Integrated Engineering Programme.

Pebble in the Pond (first week)
- UCL Engineering describes this as a special project in the first week of DPS.
- A UCL blog post from October 2022 describes the format: small teams each build part of a larger "machine" that has to carry a pebble from one side of a room to the other, using simple materials such as cardboard, tape, elastic bands, paper and wood. The team work takes a few hours and the activity is run several times in the first week because no single room can hold every student. Details may differ in your year.
- It is partly an icebreaker, but its aims are serious: collaboration, design thinking, communication and learning from mistakes. It shows the design–build–test–modify cycle in miniature and makes a key point about large projects: sub-systems built by different teams have to fit together (systems integration).
- How to get the most from it: agree the interface early (where your part receives the pebble, at what height and speed, and where it hands it on), build a rough version quickly, test it with the neighbouring teams' parts, and iterate. Afterwards, note what went wrong and why; reflection on transferable skills is part of the exercise.

Scenarios (week-long projects)
- During a Scenario week, other lectures stop and you work in a team on one technical engineering design project, applying what you have learned in DPS. Because DPS is taught in discipline cohorts, expect a mechanical engineering problem, but check the brief for your year.
- UCL's pages do not say exactly when the Scenarios fall in your year, so check your timetable.
- A week is short. Successful teams typically:
  - read the brief together on day one and turn it into a short list of checkable requirements;
  - split the work into tasks with owners and a simple schedule ending before the deadline, leaving time to assemble the report or presentation;
  - generate more than one concept and choose using agreed criteria (for example a weighted decision matrix);
  - support the chosen design with calculations, sketches or CAD and, where relevant, a risk assessment;
  - keep one shared document and agree a common style for figures, units and references.
- Present the design so that a non-specialist can follow the problem, the chosen solution and why it was chosen, with clear limitations and next steps.

Common pitfalls
- Spending most of the week on research and leaving no time to design.
- Choosing a concept before defining the requirements.
- Dividing the report so that sections contradict each other (different loads, units or assumptions).
- Forgetting to check calculations for units and order of magnitude.

Exam tips: in Scenario reports, a short table linking each requirement to the design feature and evidence that meets it is an efficient way to show the marker that the brief has been answered.

UCL lists engineering drawing and CAD among the technical skills taught in DPS. In the UK, technical product documentation is governed by BS 8888, whose current edition is BS 8888:2025; it draws on international (ISO) drawing standards. The points below are the basics you will use from the first week.

Orthographic projection
- An object is shown by several 2D views (typically front, plan and end), each looking straight at one face.
- First-angle projection: each view is drawn on the opposite side of the front view from where it is seen. The plan (view from above) is placed below the front view, and the view from the left is placed on the right.
- Third-angle projection: each view is drawn on the same side as it is seen from. The plan goes above the front view, and the view from the left goes on the left.
- A drawing must show which method it uses, with the standard projection symbol in the title block.

Line types (common conventions)
- Continuous thick lines: visible outlines and edges.
- Dashed thin lines: hidden detail.
- Thin chain lines (long dash, dot): centre lines and axes of symmetry.
- Continuous thin lines: dimension lines, projection lines and hatching.

Sections
- A section view shows the object as if cut along a cutting plane, revealing internal features. Cut material is hatched with thin lines, usually at 45°.

Dimensioning and tolerances
- Linear dimensions are normally given in millimetres, and the unit is stated once on the drawing rather than after every number.
- Dimension each feature once, enough to define it fully, with no redundant chains.
- Dimension from functional datums (the faces or holes that locate the part in an assembly).
- No part can be made to an exact size, so tolerances state the acceptable variation (for example 25 ± 0.1 mm). Tighter tolerances cost more, so only make them tight where function requires.

Title block and scale
- Includes part name, drawing number, material, scale (for example 1:2 or 2:1), projection symbol, units, author, date and revision.

CAD workflow (general)
- Sketch 2D profiles, then constrain them fully with dimensions and geometric relations (parallel, tangent, coincident) so that the geometry matches the design intent.
- Turn sketches into 3D features: extrude, revolve, cut, fillet, chamfer, pattern.
- Combine parts into assemblies using mates or joints, and check for interference.
- Produce 2D drawings from the model; the drawing, not the model, is often the contractual document for manufacture.
- Name features sensibly and keep the feature tree tidy so that others can edit the model.

Exam tips: in drawing tasks, marks are often lost on missing projection symbols, inconsistent line types, double dimensioning and missing units or scale, rather than on the geometry itself.

notes.h: Ethics, risk assessment and professional responsibility
notes.body:
DPS includes ethics, professional standards, sustainability, risk and safety. These are areas where there is genuine factual content worth knowing precisely.

The Statement of Ethical Principles
- The Engineering Council and the Royal Academy of Engineering publish a joint Statement of Ethical Principles for the engineering profession. It was first published over 20 years ago and was updated in February 2026.
- The updated statement has five principles:
  1. Honesty and integrity.
  2. Responsibility to society.
  3. Accuracy and rigour.
  4. Leadership and communication.
  5. Responsibility for the future of technology, society and the environment (the new, fifth principle added in the 2026 update).
- Use these headings to structure ethics discussions in reports: name the principle, explain how it applies to the case, and say what a responsible engineer would do.

Approaching an ethics case
- Identify the facts, the stakeholders and the decision to be made.
- Identify the principles or duties in tension (for example meeting a deadline against public safety).
- Consider options and their consequences, including speaking up through proper channels.
- Reach a justified recommendation and state what would change your view.

Risk assessment
- A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm; a risk is the combination of how likely that harm is and how severe it would be.
- The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) sets out five steps for managing risk: identify hazards; assess the risks; control the risks; record your findings; review the controls.
- Many teams rate risk using a likelihood × severity matrix, then re-rate the residual risk after controls are applied.
- The hierarchy of control ranks measures from most to least effective: eliminate the hazard; substitute something less hazardous; engineering controls (guards, ventilation, interlocks); administrative controls (procedures, training, signage); personal protective equipment as the last line of defence.

Sustainability and professional context
- Think about the whole life cycle of a product: materials, manufacture, use, maintenance and end of life.
- Professional registration in the UK (for example as an Incorporated or Chartered Engineer) is through engineering institutions licensed by the Engineering Council, and registrants are expected to uphold professional and ethical standards.

Exam tips: in a risk assessment, be specific. "Hand caught in rotating pulley during adjustment: fit a fixed guard and isolate before adjustment" earns more credit than "moving parts: be careful".

questions.q: On a multi-view drawing, the plan (view from above) is placed directly below the front view. Which projection method is being used?
questions.why: In first-angle projection each view is drawn on the opposite side of the front view from where it is seen, so the view from above goes below. Third-angle projection places each view on the same side it is seen from, so the plan would be above the front view. Isometric and oblique projections are single pictorial views of the object, not arrangements of separate orthographic views.

questions.q: In the hierarchy of control, which measure is considered the most effective way to reduce a risk?
options: Training and written safe working procedures
questions.why: Removing the hazard means nobody can be harmed by it, so elimination sits at the top of the hierarchy. Personal protective equipment is the last resort, because it only protects the wearer and fails if it is not worn or fits badly. Training and procedures are administrative controls that rely on people always following them. A fixed guard is an engineering control: effective, but it still leaves the hazard in place, so it ranks below elimination and substitution.

questions.q: Which principle was added as the fifth principle when the Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering updated their Statement of Ethical Principles in February 2026?
options: Responsibility for the future of technology, society and the environment
questions.why: The 2026 update added a fifth principle, responsibility for the future of technology, society and the environment. Honesty and integrity, accuracy and rigour, and leadership and communication were all principles in the earlier four-principle statement, so none of them is the new addition.
